$2048 FOR FARCASTER CLIENTS

Anyone can build a Farcaster client and run a read node to get data from the protocol. There are developer tutorials on the web[1,2,3,4], but your mission in this prize, should you choose to accept it, is to improve them by collecting all relevant info and making it incredibly easy. 

Specifically, we want you to get it down to three commands, as described in your quickstart and then detailed in your tutorial:

(0) Provision necessary compute via script (1) Set up a Snapchain read node (2) Create a client that reads from that node

The read node should run on its own, with no API keys from anyone. You just furnish the compute. Note that a read node syncs the network but does not accept writes, so your client should read from your own node and submit casts to a validator endpoint; the tutorial should explain how that works.

The client should be able to import an existing seed phrase for an account that already has storage, use that seed phrase to issue the client its own app key (one small Optimism transaction), and then post with that key: read the feed, post casts, follow and react, and include/exclude casts from any other client.

In addition to the quickstart at the top of the page, the tutorial should be mobile- and desktop-friendly, and should explain key protocol concepts as it goes (e.g. FIDs, custody addresses, app keys, Snapchain messages, read nodes vs validators, storage rent). Anything that someone running a client and read node would need to know.

You can use AI, but your output must *not* be AI slop, as ultimately determined in our sole discretion. To qualify for a prize, you need to have at least one other human user successfully go through your tutorial and create a read node and client. They then need to post on Farcaster publicly vouching for the quality of your work.

You can go the extra mile of course, like adding Chinese translation, adding a 59s vertical video, and so on. But getting more humans to vouch for your tutorial will be the most powerful signal.

To enter, submit a reply to this post with three URLs: (1) your microsite with the quickstart + tutorial, (2) the associated GitHub repository with all MIT-licensed open source code, and (3) the link to your voucher's public endorsement on Farcaster.

Prize: $2,048 first place, $512 second place, $128 each for honorable mentions, subject to whether there are enough good submissions. Paid in USDC to your public Farcaster wallet address by default.

Deadline: your reply with three URLs must be submitted within seven days exactly from this post's timestamp.

That’s it! Go learn the Farcaster protocol yourself, help others learn how to boot up their own clients, earn crypto for doing it, and increase practical freedom of association.

Yo @balajis.eth the statement about entering seed phases caught my eye. 

So I asked Ai… “Is entering seed phrases safe in this context?”

> No. I would strongly discourage entering your existing Farcaster seed phrase into a new or untrusted client. It's an unnecessary security risk, especially when the purpose is simply to authorise the client to post on your behalf.

The concerning part of the prize announcement is:

"The client should be able to import an existing seed phrase for an account that already has storage, use that seed phrase to issue the client its own app key..."

This is technically possible, but it is not the security model I would recommend for onboarding users to a Farcaster client.

Why this is dangerous… (see images)

Cc @quazia

Ai continued:

> My assessment of the prize
The competition itself is not necessarily malicious. It may be encouraging developers to demonstrate complete self-custodial account management.

However, the wording encourages a potentially unsafe pattern, particularly if winners publish tutorials that normalise pasting seed phrases into unfamiliar applications.

I would recommend:
1. Never enter your primary Farcaster seed phrase into a competition demo, unfamiliar website or downloaded script.

2. For testing, use a newly generated, disposable account with no valuable assets.

3. For production clients, require wallet-based signing and delegated app keys, preferably with limited permissions and expiration.

4. Review what you're signing, even when a client doesn't request your seed phrase.

P.s: Why encourage seed phrase imports when the protocol already supports delegated signer authorisation without exposing the custody secret?

Three quick clarifications:

1. Read nodes actually *do* take writes, and send them to validator nodes. The docs got updated last week:
https://snapchain.farcaster.xyz/node-types#message-submission-and-the-mempool
https://github.com/farcasterxyz/snapchain/pull/1034

2. You *don't* need an optimism transaction anymore for app keys, as they are gasless. The docs here got updated about 2 months ago:
https://snapchain.farcaster.xyz/guides/writing-messages
https://github.com/farcasterxyz/snapchain/pull/989

3.	This is a *developer* tutorial. So: just like a Unix tutorial would describe how 'rm' works, and that it's powerful/dangerous when used recursively, and that you shouldn't use it carelessly, so too should you treat the use of seed phrases. Mention that anyone testing your tutorial should only do it from a test account, they should in general only paste seed phrases into software from devs they trust, that you want to use delegated signer authorization whenever possible, and so on.  @10xchris.eth 

Points 1 and 2 actually make your life easier — but it's possible that as more people go through the process, that there are other bits of outdated documentation. If so, please do submit any needed pull requests to the appropriate github.com/farcasterxyz repo (but please don't submit AI slop). That kind of thing will definitely help with prize-winning, and more importantly it'll help devs stand up new clients and nodes.

Curious about how to make this experiment sustainable?…

The lowest suitable configuration I could price is approximately A$103/month before tax, using Netcup in Europe. 

AWS is around A$442/month before outbound bandwidth. 

Akash’s live estimator returned A$310/month.

These are prices checked 18 October 2026.

I used Snapchain’s documented requirements—4 CPU cores, 16 GB RAM, and 2 TB free storage—and priced 2 TiB of storage for comparison. These are infrastructure estimates; actual performance and network traffic still need a running-node test.
